turns.response_html:
Since this came from a cheap fan, it is likely a 2-speed DC motor or a PSC (Permanent Split Capacitor) AC motor, rather than a stepper.

In these simple devices, the gray stripe usually identifies the negative (ground) or neutral wire within a pair. Here is the likely breakdown:

  • Pair 1: Main power connection. The wire with the gray stripe is the negative/neutral, and the solid wire is positive/hot.
  • Pair 2: Speed control or oscillation. Cheap fans often use the second pair to activate a lower speed setting or to power a secondary motor that makes the fan swing side-to-side.

To identify them safely:

  1. Check for continuity: Use a multimeter to see if the pairs are actually connected. If a pair shows low resistance (around 10-100 ohms), it is a motor coil.
  2. Look for a capacitor: If you see a small black or gray box nearby, one pair connects to that to help the motor start.

Do you have a multimeter or the fan's model name to narrow this down further?

turns.response_html:
Based on the photo you provided, you have a Shaded-Pole AC induction motor. This is the standard "workhorse" for cheap plastic fans because it is incredibly simple, durable, and inexpensive to manufacture.

The four wires are likely arranged as two distinct pairs: one for the main power and one for a secondary function like speed control or an oscillation motor.

What Your Multimeter Will Tell You

Set your multimeter to the Ohms ($\Omega$) setting. Since this is an AC motor, you are looking for continuity through the copper coils you see in the photo.

  • Checking Pair 1 (Power): Touch your probes to the two wires in the first pair (one solid, one with a gray stripe). You should see a resistance reading (likely between 50$\Omega$ and 200$\Omega$). If it reads "OL" (Open Line), the internal thermal fuse has likely blown.
  • Checking Pair 2 (Speed/Oscillation): Check the second pair. If this is a 2-speed fan, you might find that one wire from Pair 1 and one from Pair 2 show resistance, indicating they are "taps" on the same internal coil.
  • Safety Check: Touch one probe to any of the wires and the other to the metal frame of the motor. It should read OL (infinite resistance). If you see any resistance value here, the motor has a dangerous short to the frame and should not be used.

Typical Wiring Logic for These Fans

In small household fans, the gray stripe is almost always used as the Neutral or "Common" return line.

Wire AppearanceLikely FunctionConnection
Solid Black/UnmarkedLine (Hot)Connects to the Power Switch
Gray Repeating StripeNeutral (Common)Connects to the Wide blade of the AC plug
Secondary PairSpeed or SwingUsually goes to a selector switch or a small "clock" motor

A Quick Note on "Shaded-Pole"

Notice the thick single copper loops on the corners of the metal frame in your photo—those are the "shading coils." They create a delayed magnetic field that allows the motor to start spinning without needing a separate capacitor. This confirms it's a shaded-pole motor and not a stepper or PSC motor.
